A build-along course

Building StrikeFlow

A production-grade marketing site, built from an empty folder to a tested, deployable app — with SvelteKit 3, Svelte 5, TypeScript in strict mode, vanilla CSS, TradingView charts, and an SEO layer built to actually rank.

27 chapters SvelteKit 3 RC Svelte 5 TypeScript strict
Start chapter 01 →

Everything we'll cover

  1. 01 What we're building A tour of the finished site, what you need installed, and how to get the most out of this course.
  2. 02 Scaffolding the project One command creates the project. We go through every flag, then take a tour of what it gave us.
  3. 03 What's different in SvelteKit 3 Five changes that will trip you up if you've used SvelteKit 2, and that every tutorial you find online still gets wrong.
  4. 04 TypeScript, tightened Two extra compiler flags that catch real crashes, and the one setting SvelteKit 3 now requires you to write yourself.
  5. 05 Fonts, done properly Getting Montserrat and Sofia Sans on the page is easy. Getting them there without a flash of jumping text is where the engineering is.
  6. 06 Design tokens One file that owns every colour, size and duration in the project — and the breakpoint scale we build everything on.
  7. 07 Reset, base and utilities Flatten the browser defaults, restyle raw HTML, and add the small handful of layout helpers we will actually reuse.
  8. 08 The data layer Typed constants that every page and every piece of structured data reads from. One source of truth, no drift.
  9. 09 Environment variables SvelteKit 3 replaced implicit `$env/*` imports with declared, validated, type-safe variables. This is a genuine upgrade.
  10. 10 The SEO component One component that owns everything inside <head> a search engine or social crawler reads — with required props, so you cannot forget one.
  11. 11 Structured data that actually connects Most tutorials give you four disconnected JSON-LD blocks. We build one @graph where every node references the others by @id.
  12. 12 sitemap.xml, robots.txt and llms.txt Three generated files, and a clear explanation of what each one actually controls — including the distinction almost everyone gets wrong.
  13. 13 UI primitives Button, Card, Badge and Logo — and the single most important accessibility rule in front-end work.
  14. 14 The header and a mobile drawer that is not broken A sticky header, and a slide-in navigation drawer built on <dialog> — which gives us focus trapping, Escape and inertness for free.
  15. 15 The layout and the HTML shell Wire up the global stylesheet, add the skip link and main landmark, and put the single most valuable performance tag in the document head.
  16. 16 A TradingView chart, wired up properly Lightweight Charts v5 in a Svelte component — using {@attach}, a dynamic import, and deterministic data so hydration never disagrees with the server.
  17. 17 Marketing components Section headers, the feature grid, stat strips, CTA bands, an FAQ accordion with no JavaScript, and a pricing table.
  18. 18 The home page Assembling the components into a page — and writing a headline that works for both humans and search engines.
  19. 19 Features, pricing, about and contact Four more pages, built from the same components — plus the section that makes a financial site trustworthy.
  20. 20 Lead capture: the server side Storage behind an interface, HMAC-signed expiring tokens, and rate limiting — the three pieces before we touch the form.
  21. 21 The remote form SvelteKit 3's `form()` — a server function you import into a component, that works with JavaScript disabled.
  22. 22 The capture page Wiring the form into markup, showing validation errors accessibly, hiding a honeypot properly — and the one page that cannot be prerendered.
  23. 23 The gated download Validate the token on the server, serve the PDF from outside `static/`, and generate the PDF itself with headless Chromium.
  24. 24 The blog and the legal pages Dynamic routes with `entries()`, article structured data, a nested layout, and why a trading site needs a risk disclosure.
  25. 25 Unit tests Testing the security-critical code — and writing the one test that would catch a forged token.
  26. 26 End-to-end tests, and the two bugs they found Testing SEO metadata, the no-JavaScript path, and the gated download — plus a true story about how these tests caught two real defects.
  27. 27 Ship it The full verification pipeline, deployment with adapter-node, and a pre-launch checklist worth actually running.

Every chapter shows the real code from the finished project. Type it out rather than pasting where you can — the errors you make and fix are the part that sticks.
